segments: The command interfaces in this article have been checked against the official Distrobox 1.8.2.5 scripts. Image tags and distribution package names are examples; before using them, confirm that the image is still supported, its repositories are available, and the versions match your system. The examples have not been tested by running them.

This article is a handbook-style reference for everyday Distrobox use, covering image pulls, container creation, entering and exiting containers, lifecycle management, and special container modes. All commands use the full parameter forms; the original Chinese notes explain each flag.
1. Image management
Where images come from
Distrobox does not maintain its own operating system images. It directly uses container images compatible with the OCI (Open Container Initiative) standard. Sources include:
Image source
Example
Description
Default source; no registry needs to be specified
Images built specifically for the Toolbx family
Maintained by communities such as Universal Blue
Official Fedora images

When --image is omitted, Distrobox uses the configured default image. It does not infer Ubuntu from --name ubuntu. The name and image are independent parameters. Specify the image explicitly in production; version tags can still be updated, so strict pinning requires an image digest and package repository snapshots.
Pulling images
When creating a container, Distrobox automatically pulls the corresponding image from the registry if it is not available locally:
You can also pull the image manually before creating the container:
The risk of the :latest tag :latest is a floating tag: each pull may retrieve a different version. Always pin the version number in production:
Recommended: ubuntu:24.04
Avoid: ubuntu:latest
Distrobox 1.7.0 automatically appends :latest to images without a tag, so --image ubuntu is equivalent to --image ubuntu:latest and is likewise not recommended.
Viewing downloaded images

distrobox list does not list images on their own; it lists containers created from those images. To manage the images themselves, use the underlying container engine's commands (podman images / docker images).
2. Container lifecycle (core commands)
These are the five groups of core commands you will use every day. Mastering them covers 90% of routine operations.

Practical examples

About --additional-packages Distrobox automatically detects the distribution's package manager inside the container (apt/dnf/pacman/apk/zypper, etc.) and uses it to install the packages you specify. You generally do not need to install these basic tools manually afterward, but create itself only creates the container. Package installation happens during the first enter/initialization process; assemble's start/export operations may also trigger initialization.

--root vs rootless --root makes the backend use host root privileges and separate rootful container storage. The guest's login user is a separate setting. Use the default rootless mode for the vast majority of everyday tasks (omit --root); it matches the host user's privileges and is safer.

Practical examples

Checking whether you are inside a container
After entering a container, you can check the following environment variables:
$CONTAINER_ID: contains the container name (such as mybox); empty outside the container
$DISTROBOX_ENTER_PATH: the host's working directory path when you entered the container
The output of hostname includes the container name
Use echo $CONTAINER_ID to quickly check whether you are currently inside a Distrobox container.

When to use --no-workdir By default, distrobox enter tries to map the host's current $PWD to the same path inside the container and automatically cd there. This is very convenient in the following scenario:
If that path does not exist inside the container, however (for example, a custom host path), Distrobox falls back to $HOME. Use --no-workdir to skip this automatic mapping behavior.
distrobox list: view containers
Output columns
Column name
Meaning
Short hexadecimal representation of the underlying engine's container ID
Container name (the --name specified at creation; human-readable)
Runtime status: Up (running) or Exited (stopped)
OCI image address used at creation
Example output:
For everyday operations, the container name is sufficient. The short IDs in the list come from the underlying OCI container engine; they are not sequential numbers assigned by Distrobox.
distrobox stop / distrobox rm: stop and remove containers
Description
Supported by both stop and rm; applies only to the selected backend and root mode
Force removal (rm); use --yes to skip interactive confirmation
Check your data before removing a container distrobox rm permanently deletes the container and its filesystem changes (excluding the home directory shared through a mount). Before removing it, check:
Whether custom configuration inside the container has been backed up
Whether important uncommitted data has been moved to the host

The home directory is shared by default, so files under ~ on the host are not lost when a container is removed. If you use a separate --home, however, you are responsible for managing that path; --rm-home deletes qualifying custom home directories, which need separate backups. rm also asks the backend to remove associated anonymous volumes, so check volume data separately.
distrobox upgrade: upgrade containers
What does upgrade actually do? Distrobox automatically detects the distribution inside the container and uses its native package manager to run update + upgrade:
Distribution
Equivalent command

The upgrade targets the guest's package database and filesystem; it does not upgrade NixOS through the host's package manager. Package scripts may still access the shared HOME, sockets, network, or host-exec. “Complete isolation” is not a security guarantee.
Description
Upgrade all existing containers
Upgrade rootful containers
3. Special container modes
Ephemeral containers (disposable temporary containers)
distrobox-ephemeral creates disposable containers and automatically removes the temporary container when you exit. This does not undo changes to the image cache, shared HOME, volumes, or host.
Full syntax:
Parameter descriptions
distrobox-ephemeral accepts almost the same parameters as distrobox create (--name, --image, --additional-packages, --home, --root, etc.), with these differences:
No need to specify --name (a random name is generated automatically if omitted)
After you exit, the container is destroyed automatically; there is no need to run distrobox rm
Practical examples
Best uses for ephemeral containers
Disposable userspace experiments: test only trusted programs; dangerous commands can still affect shared host data
One-off builds: fetch the source, compile it, and take the output without leaving build dependencies behind
Version comparisons: quickly run the same command on different distributions and compare behavior
Tool isolation: temporarily use a tool that is not installed on the host (such as ffmpeg), then discard the container
Every ephemeral container starts fresh from the image, so network download overhead depends on whether --image is already cached locally.
distrobox-host-exec: run host commands from inside a container
This is a special tool: while inside a container, you can use it to run commands on the host.
Full syntax (used inside the container):
Practical examples

Why use host-exec? A core principle of Distrobox containers is close integration with the host (sharing HOME, X11/Wayland, D-Bus, and more), but the guest's package database and running services are separate from the host's. To manage the host's Flatpak or systemd, explicitly invoke commands on the host so that you do not mistake guest administration commands for host operations.
distrobox-host-exec provides this "bridge": while working inside a container, you can seamlessly invoke host GUI applications, service management commands, clipboard tools, and more.
Inside the container, it is implemented as a shell script at /usr/bin/distrobox-host-exec (the guest injection path used by the 1.8.2.5 creation process).

host-exec uses host-spawn as a bridge. Commands actually execute on the host, and their privileges and effects on data belong to the host as well. If the guest's working directory is a path such as /run/host/... that does not exist on the host, explicitly choose a directory available on the host rather than misreading ENOENT as a missing program.

File sharing and home directory separation
Distrobox shares the host's HOME directory with the container by default. This means:
Running ls ~/Documents inside the container shows the files on the host
If you git clone into ~/projects/ in the container, the files are also visible back on the host
Different containers naturally share files through the HOME directory
Sharing HOME also has a drawback: dotfiles from different distributions can conflict. For example, Arch and Ubuntu may expect different configuration in ~/.bashrc.
The solution is to assign a separate HOME directory to each distribution.
Separate HOME vs shared HOME: trade-offs
Mode
Advantages
Disadvantages
Shared HOME (default)
Files are shared naturally, with no extra configuration
Distribution-specific dotfiles may interfere with one another
Separate HOME (--home)
Clean separation of dotfiles; suitable for using multiple distributions side by side
Changes HOME's default location; the host's original home is still mounted, so this does not provide file security isolation
Recommended approach: share HOME for your main everyday container and use a separate HOME for special-purpose containers, such as those used to test behavior across distributions.
Custom HOME + --volume: organize configuration and project paths

--home changes the guest's HOME and the default location of its dotfiles, but 1.8.2.5 still mounts the host's original home, which can be identified through DISTROBOX_HOST_HOME. cd ~ → enter the container's separate ~/distrobox-homes/arch
cd /host-home → access the host's actual home directory

The manifest field is volume, which accepts repeated declarations or a space-separated list; it is not additional_volumes or a semicolon-separated list.
Key points to watch
--volume is read-write by default, so changes inside the container are reflected on the host. Add :ro for read-only access.
With rootless Podman, UID mappings match by default, so reading and writing the home directory generally works without issues.
--home determines where $HOME points; --volume determines which additional directories are exposed. They are independent and can be combined.
After changing volume in the ini file, run distrobox rm arch and recreate the container for the change to take effect.
A plain distrobox rm arch does not delete the separate home directory (~/distrobox-homes/arch); that happens only when you add --rm-home.

These automatic integrations make Distrobox containers feel very close to a "native environment", without the tedious manual --device and --volume mounts typically required by Docker.
